blocks.x: Basic Medical Chemistry · Organic Functional Groups

Two closely related functional-group families: alkyl halides (R–X) and alcohols (R–OH). Alcohols are the major route to alkyl halides, and alkyl halides are the major route back to alcohols — so this module treats them together, exactly as the source lecture does.

2substitution mechanisms (SN1 & SN2) and 2 elimination mechanisms (E1 & E2) shared by both functional groups 3classes of carbon substitution — primary, secondary, tertiary — used to classify both alkyl halides and alcohols HI > HBr > HCl >> HForder of reactivity among hydrogen halides, driven by C–X bond strength
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to…

items: 1Classify and name alkyl halides and alcohols — as primary, secondary or tertiary, and by both IUPAC and common nomenclature.
2Relate structure to physical properties — boiling point, density and solubility trends for R–X and R–OH compared with the parent alkane.
3Explain the synthesis routes for alkyl halides (from alkanes, alkenes and alcohols) and for alcohols (hydration of alkenes; reduction of carbonyls; Grignard reactions).
4Distinguish SN1 from SN2 and E1 from E2 — mechanism, rate law, stereochemistry, and the substrate/nucleophile/solvent factors that favour each pathway.
5Describe the key reactions of alcohols — with metals, oxidation, dehydration, esterification and conversion to alkyl halides.
6Recognise the commercial and pharmaceutical significance of organohalogen compounds (PVC, DDT, chloramphenicol, Freons) and alcoholic compounds (disinfectants, solvents, beverages).

blocks.x: Core definitions

Alkyl halide (haloalkane) A compound with a halogen substituent (fluoro, chloro, bromo or iodo) bonded to an alkyl group. General formula R–X, where R is alkyl and X = F, Cl, Br or I. Example: CH3CH2Br (ethyl bromide / bromoethane).
Alcohol An organic compound whose functional group is the hydroxyl group, –OH. General formula R–OH.

Primary / secondary / tertiary classification For both R–X and R–OH, the class is based on how many other carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the halogen/hydroxyl: one other carbon = primary (1°), two = secondary (2°), three = tertiary (3°). No other carbon attached = methyl halide / methanol.

Nucleophile & electrophile A nucleophile ("nucleus lover") is an electron-rich reagent that donates an electron pair to form a bond. An electrophile ("electron lover") is an electron-poor reagent (often a cation) that seeks electrons. The carbon of a polarised C–X bond is an electrophilic site attacked by nucleophiles.
Alkane / Alkene→ R–X (Alkyl Halide)↔ R–OH (Alcohol)→ Alkene / Ether / Carbonyl

Alkyl Halides · Part 1

Halogen derivatives of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and arenes are named alkyl halides (haloalkanes), alkenyl halides (haloalkenes), alkynyl halides (haloalkynes) and aryl halides (halobenzenes), respectively.
Primary, secondary & tertiary alkyl halides
Classification is based on the carbon atom to which the halogen is directly attached:
1° — Primary
The carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to only one other carbon.
2° — Secondary
The carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to two other carbons.
3° — Tertiary
The carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to three other carbons.
If the carbon bearing the halogen is bonded to no other carbon atoms, the compound is a methyl halide (e.g. CH3Cl).
Carbon–halogen bond length & strength

items: C–X bond length increases and bond strength decreases going down the halogen group (F → Cl → Br → I).
Fluoroalkanes have the strongest bond and shortest C–X bond, so they are highly resistant to bond-breaking and are the least reactive.
Order of reactivity among the hydrogen halides: HI > HBr > HCl >> HF.
Halogen atom size increases down the periodic table — fluorine is smallest, iodine largest.

blocks.x: IUPAC system
Alkyl halides are named as haloalkanes — the halogen is treated as a substituent (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-) on a parent alkane chain.

items: The longest alkyl chain is the parent.
Number the chain in the direction giving the substituted carbon the lowest number.
Assign each substituent a locant according to its position, and list substituents in alphabetical order.
If either end gives the same lowest locant set, begin numbering at the end nearer the substituent that comes first alphabetically.

blocks.x: Common names
Useful only for small alkyl groups: the alkyl group is treated as a substituent on "halide". Examples: methyl fluoride, pentyl chloride, cyclohexyl iodide.
Common halogenated solvents:

items: CH<sub>2</sub>X<sub>2</sub> = methylene halide (e.g. CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, methylene chloride)
CHX<sub>3</sub> = haloform (e.g. CHCl<sub>3</sub>, chloroform)
CX<sub>4</sub> = carbon tetrahalide (e.g. CCl<sub>4</sub>, carbon tetrachloride)

blocks.x: Caution: many chloroalkanes, including CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub> and CCl<sub>4</sub>, are cumulatively toxic and carcinogenic — they should be used only in fume hoods, with care.

Alkyl Halides · Part 2
Compared with the parent alkane R–H, an alkyl halide R–X is heavier, more polar, and carries a reactive, electrophilic carbon.
Boiling point, solubility & density

c: Higher than alkanes of similar carbon number (greater molecular weight + more polar). For isomeric halides, boiling point decreases as branching increases.
Polar, but insoluble in water — cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. Soluble in typical organic solvents.
Alkyl fluorides & mono-chlorides: less dense than water (1.00 g/mL). Chlorides with ≥2 Cl atoms, and all bromides & iodides: denser than water.

blocks.x: Worked comparison — RX vs. its parent alkane RH (a) RX has a higher boiling point (larger molecular weight, more polar). (b) RX is more dense (heavy X atom); density order RI > RBr > RCl > RF. (c) RX, like RH, is insoluble in water.
Electronegativity & reactivity

items: The C–X bond is polarised: halogens are more electronegative than carbon.
Carbon bears a partial positive charge (δ+); the halogen bears a partial negative charge (δ−).
This makes the carbon an electrophilic site, open to attack by a nucleophile — the basis of all substitution chemistry covered next.

blocks.x: Four routes to alkyl halides

1HalogenationAlkanes + Cl<sub>2</sub> or Br<sub>2</sub> gas, with UV radiation (free-radical mechanism). 2From alcoholsROH + HX, PX<sub>3</sub>, or SOCl<sub>2</sub> (the major method — see below). 3HX additionHX adds across the double bond of an alkene. 4X<sub>2</sub> additionX<sub>2</sub> (Br or Cl) + alkene → a vicinal dihalide.
Preparing alkyl halides from alcohols
1. Alcohols + hydrogen halides (HCl, HBr, HI) — a substitution in which halogen replaces the hydroxyl group as a substituent on carbon.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH + HCl → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl + H–OH

This tertiary-alcohol reaction proceeds by an SN1 mechanism through a carbocation intermediate. Reactivity order of alcohols: tertiary > secondary > primary (tertiary alcohols are the most reactive, primary the least).
2. Thionyl chloride:
R–OH + SOCl<sub>2</sub> → R–Cl + SO<sub>2</sub> + HCl
3. Phosphorus halides:
3 R–OH + PX<sub>3</sub> → 3 R–X + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> (X = Cl or Br)

sections.title: SN1 vs. SN2 at a glance

blocks.x: Alkyl Halides · Part 3
Alkyl halides undergo two competing reaction types. In substitution, X is replaced by a nucleophile; in elimination (dehydrohalogenation), H–X is lost and an alkene forms.
Substitution R–X → R–OH + X− (general: R–X + Nu− → R–Nu + X−). The expelled halide anion is called the leaving group.

Elimination
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub> + HBr. Elements of H and X leave adjacent carbons, forming a C=C double bond (an alkene) via dehydrohalogenation.
SN1 vs. SN2 at a glance
SN1 — Unimolecular

items: Two steps. Step 1 (slow, r.d.s.): R–X ionises to a carbocation R+ and X−. Step 2 (fast): carbocation + Nu− → R–Nu.
Rate law: Rate = k[R–X] — depends on one species only.
Favoured by stable carbocations: 3° > 2° > 1° (1° carbocations are too unstable, so 1° halides do not undergo SN1).
Stereochemistry: racemisation — the planar carbocation is attacked from either face, giving a ~50:50 mix of R and S enantiomers.

blocks.x: SN2 — Bimolecular

items: One step. Nu− attacks carbon as X− leaves, via a pentacoordinate transition state.
Rate law: Rate = k[R–X][Nu−] — depends on both species.
Reactivity order: 1° > 2° > 3° (opposite to SN1) — bulky groups sterically block backside attack; 3° halides do not undergo SN2.
Nucleophile approaches the C–X bond at 180° (backside attack).
Stereochemistry: inversion (Walden inversion) — an R-enantiomer converts to the S-enantiomer.

blocks.x: Q: Which reacts faster in an SN1 reaction — isopropyl bromide (2°) or isobutyl bromide (1°)?
A: Isopropyl bromide. The SN1 rate-determining step is carbocation formation, and secondary carbocations are more stable than primary ones.
E1 vs. E2 mechanisms
E1 — Unimolecular

Two-step, shares its first step with SN1: slow ionisation of R–X to a carbocation, then a base removes a β-proton to give the alkene. Favoured by the same conditions as SN1 (polar protic solvent, stable carbocation, branched substrate, good leaving group, weak/absent nucleophile). Higher temperature favours E1.
E2 — Bimolecular

One step, like SN2: the base removes the β-hydrogen at the same time the leaving group departs and the C=C double bond forms — no intermediate. A strong, bulky base favours E2 over SN2, since it cannot easily approach the backside of the α-carbon for inline attack.
Tips to draw a dehydrohalogenation product: (1) find the α-carbon (bears X); (2) identify β-carbons bearing H; (3) remove X and a β-H, forming a π bond between them.
Common bases (alkoxides) used: NaOH, KOH, NaOCH3 (sodium methoxide), NaOCH2CH3 (sodium ethoxide), KOC(CH3)3 (potassium tert-butoxide).
Substitution or elimination?
Because SN1 and E1 occur under similar conditions, they are competitive and hard to direct exclusively toward one pathway.
Alkyl Halides · Part 4
Beyond simple R–X compounds, halogens also appear bonded to carbonyl carbons, alkene carbons and aromatic rings — with major commercial and pharmaceutical applications.
Acyl, vinyl & aryl halides
Acyl halide
Halogen bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon.
Vinyl halide
Halogen bonded to an alkene carbon.
Aryl halide
Halogen bonded to a carbon on a benzene ring.
Commercially & pharmaceutically significant organohalogens
PVCVinyl chloride (H2C=CHCl) — polymerised to polyvinyl chloride. Rigid PVC: pipes, doors/windows, bottles, cards. Soft PVC (with plasticisers): plumbing, cable insulation, imitation leather.

DDTDichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane — formed by condensing chlorobenzene and chloral in conc. H2SO4. A highly toxic synthetic insecticide, acting as a contact poison that disorganises the insect nervous system.
CAPChloramphenicol — a broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic, effective against most Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic organisms.
CFCFreons (e.g. CCl3F, CCl2F2) — 20th-century refrigerants, now limited due to ozone-depletion effects; replaced by ammonia, SO2, or non-halogenated hydrocarbons like propane.
Germicides using halogenated compounds are used as skin disinfectants and in mothballs.
Structure A = primary carbocation, B = tertiary, C = secondary. Order of increasing stability: A < C < B (more alkyl substitution stabilises the positive charge through hyperconjugation/induction).

blocks.x: SN1 (tertiary butyl chloride): unimolecular, Rate = k[RX]; carbocation intermediate; nucleophilic attack from either face gives racemic product.
SN2 (1-butyl chloride, primary): bimolecular, Rate = k[RX][Nu]; pentacoordinate transition state; sterically hindered halides cannot react this way.
Alcohols · Part 1
Alcohols are organic compounds characterised by the hydroxyl group, –OH. General formula R–OH.
Primary, secondary & tertiary alcohols
Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on whether the –OH is attached to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon — exactly as alkyl halides are classified.
CH3CH2CH2CH2OH — 1-butanol (n-butanol), 1° CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 — 2-butanol (sec-butyl alcohol), 2° CH3C(CH3)2OH — 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol), 3°
All three share the same molecular formula, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH — illustrating how classification depends on connectivity, not just formula.
IUPAC system

items: Replace the final "e" of the parent hydrocarbon name with "ol."
The parent hydrocarbon is the longest continuous chain containing the –OH.
Number the chain to give the –OH the lowest possible number.
Two –OH groups → add "diol" to the parent name.
More than one substituent → list them in alphabetical order.

blocks.x: Examples from the lecture: 1-pentanol; 5-chloro-2-methyl-2-pentanol; 5-methyl-3-hexanol; 7-methyl-3,5-octanediol; 4,4-dimethyl-1-cyclohexanol.
Common (functional class) names
Simple alcohols are often called by common names (also approved by IUPAC): name the alkyl group bearing the –OH, then add "alcohol" as a separate word.
Alcohols · Part 2
Hydrogen bonding is the defining feature of alcohol physical behaviour — it explains why alcohols boil far higher than alkanes or alkyl halides of similar weight.
Boiling point, solubility & density

c: Much higher than alkanes/alkyl halides of similar molecular weight — alcohol molecules associate through intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

Depends on alkyl-group size: <4 carbons → soluble in water; >4 carbons → insoluble. Branched alkyl groups are more soluble than unbranched (less nonpolar surface contact) — e.g. tert-butyl alcohol > n-butyl alcohol in water solubility.
All liquid alcohols: ~0.8 g/mL — less dense than water.

blocks.x:
Worked comparison
(a) Propanol boils higher than the corresponding hydrocarbon because it can hydrogen-bond intermolecularly. (b) Propanol (unlike propane/butane) is soluble in H<sub>2</sub>O because it can hydrogen-bond with water. (c) n-Hexanol is not water-soluble — as the R group grows, ROH behaves more like the hydrocarbon.
Five routes to alcohols

1HydrationWater adds across an alkene's double bond — Markovnikov or anti-Markovnikov manner. 2Reduce aldehyde/ketoneH<sub>2</sub> + Pt/Pd/Ni/Ru catalyst, or complex hydrides LiAlH<sub>4</sub> / NaBH<sub>4</sub>. 3Reduce carboxylic acidGives a primary alcohol; requires a strong reducing agent — LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is standard. 4Reduce esterLiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives two alcohols (e.g. methyl benzoate → benzyl alcohol + methanol). 5Grignard reactionRMgX + carbonyl compound → alcohol (see below).

Reducing agents: lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) is a very strong reducing agent that reduces many functional groups besides aldehydes/ketones. Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) is much weaker and essentially reduces only aldehydes and ketones.
Building 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols from RMgX
+ Formaldehyde
Grignard reagent + HCHO → primary alcohol.
+ Other aldehyde
Grignard reagent + RCHO → secondary alcohol.
+ Ketone
Grignard reagent + R2C=O → tertiary alcohol.

sections.title: With metals — forming alkoxides (Williamson ether synthesis)

blocks.x: Alcohols · Part 3
The oxygen of an alcohol polarises both the C–O and O–H bonds, making alcohols weak acids at the O–H bond and poor leaving groups (as OH<sup>−</sup>) at the C–O bond.

Acidity of alcohols Polarisation of the O–H bond makes the hydrogen partially positive, so alcohols are weak acids. Acid strength order: methyl alcohol > 1° > 2° > 3° alcohol. OH− is a strong base (lone pairs on O) and therefore a very poor leaving group.
With metals — forming alkoxides (Williamson ether synthesis)

2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2 Na → 2 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>
C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>–Cl → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O–CH<sub>3</sub> + NaCl
Losing H<sup>+</sup> (acting as an acid) gives the alkoxide ion RO<sup>−</sup>, which then reacts with a primary alkyl halide to form an ether.
Oxidation of alcohols

c: PCC / PDC (Cr(VI), anhydrous) stops at aldehyde; KMnO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> gives the acid
No reaction (no H on the C–OH carbon)

blocks.x: Other oxidants noted: Collins reagent (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> in pyridine); Jones reagent (chromic acid in acetone); KMnO<sub>4</sub> and nitric acid (strong oxidisers). Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) and pyridinium dichromate (PDC), both in CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, allow clean isolation of aldehydes from 1° alcohols.
Dehydration of alcohols
Heating an alcohol with strong acid removes H and OH from adjacent carbons to form an alkene.

items: Primary alcohols are the most difficult to dehydrate.
Secondary alcohols dehydrate under milder conditions.
Tertiary alcohols dehydrate under extremely mild conditions.

blocks.x: Ease of dehydration parallels the stability of the intermediate carbocation — the same trend seen in E1 elimination of alkyl halides.
Esterification & conversion back to alkyl halides
Esterification
Alcohols react with carboxylic acids, acid anhydrides, or acid chlorides to form esters.
Reaction with HX

R–OH + H–X → R–X + H–OH
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + H<sub>2</sub>O
Halide ions are good nucleophiles; PCl<sub>5</sub> and PCl<sub>3</sub> can also be used.

items: Oxidise a 1° alcohol to a carboxylic acid: KMnO4 or H2CrO4.
Reduce a carboxylic acid to a 1° alcohol: LiAlH4.
Oxidise a 1° alcohol to an aldehyde (stop there): PCC.
Reduce an aldehyde to a 1° alcohol: NaBH4 (preferred) or LiAlH4.

blocks.x: Alcoholic solvents, disinfectants & beverages
ABS. ALC.Absolute alcohol — 100% C2H5OH, containing no water.
DISINF.Alcoholic disinfectants (ethanol, isopropyl alcohol) — evaporate quickly, dissolve lipids and denature the proteins of infecting organisms.
RECT.Rectified spirit — 95.5% ethyl alcohol, 4.5% water.
MET. SP.Methylated spirit (denatured alcohol) — rectified spirit made poisonous with 4–10% methyl alcohol, pyridine traces and copper sulphate.
Other common laboratory alcoholic solvents: isopropyl alcohol, butanol, methanol. Alcoholic beverages typically contain 2–50% alcohol (ethanol) by volume.
